summary: The developer machine has the essential runtime, the DocumentDB MCP data-plane server, and Microsoft Learn search available, plus the DocumentDB agent skills. The build can start: Python, node, docker and the documentdb MCP server are present, and the sample cluster is reachable per the run-environment. Missing accelerators and a few ambiguous or outdated 'cold' facts require the builder to follow the corrected facts below; none are showstoppers for implementing the sample. Additions that would speed development: the DocumentDB Agent Kit skill. A few knowledge items (embedding model & dims, exact index parameters for 10k vectors, and pinned runtime versions) are not answered by installed skills and should be decided by the builder before coding.
summary_points: All required runtime tools to write and run the Python FastAPI + Beanie sample are present (python, pip, node, npx, docker, az), and the documentdb MCP server is available to inspect the live cluster and manage indexes.

Key installed DocumentDB skills (driver, vector-search, local-deployment, indexing, connection) provide authoritative guidance for driver patterns, index creation, local dev, and vector search syntax.

Multiple cold answers were partly wrong or outdated (resource type name, CLI group, connection-string patterns, local dev image, vector index creation syntax); the correct facts and authoritative docs are cited and must be followed by the builder.
One accelerator that would materially speed work (DocumentDB Agent Kit) is missing; install via 'npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit' if you want faster, opinionated templates and samples.

Minor tooling gaps (azd, bicep, terraform, mongosh, dotnet) are present but not blocking — they are recommended for convenience or broader CI work but not required to build this sample against the existing cluster.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (cluster-level): Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters (account-level resource: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Cluster resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (note: the resource-type name is 'mongoClusters', not 'mongodbClusters').

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used 'mongodbClusters' (an easy-to-mistype token) instead of the documented 'mongoClusters' resource-type name; older internal docs and variants can show slightly different spellings.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Bicep resource type name will make automated infra templates fail to deploy or target the wrong resource; scripts that query az resource --resource-type may not find the cluster.
improvements: Fix all published quickstarts and example ARM/Bicep snippets to use 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' consistently (Learn pages already do this; ensure any agent-kit templates use the same).
In the CLI reference page, add a short note clarifying the exact resource-type token ('mongoClusters') to avoid 'mongodbClusters' typos.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). For MongoDB-cluster-specific operations use subcommands under az cosmosdb mongodb cluster (e.g. az cosmosdb mongodb cluster create).
confusions.grounded_answer: There are two related command groups in the official docs: 'az documentdb mongocluster' and 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' (both appear in the CLI docs). The authoritative, up-to-date docs show 'az documentdb mongocluster' (and 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' also exists as an alias/parallel group). Use the published 'az documentdb mongocluster' commands where available and follow the CLI docs for your installed CLI version; both live in the (core + preview extensions) Azure CLI surface.

grounding_links.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster CLI doc
az documentdb mongocluster CLI doc

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: CLI command groups have evolved; historically some cosmosdb commands covered Mongo clusters and the 'documentdb' group now exposes the dedicated cluster commands. Both names appear in docs, causing ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: Both 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' and 'az documentdb mongocluster' CLI docs

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong az command group may fail on some CLI versions or require installing a specific CLI extension; scripts must detect which command group the installed CLI exposes.
improvements: Document in the agent kit which az command group to prefer (e.g., 'az documentdb mongocluster') and provide a small detection snippet that falls back if a synonym group is present.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters (or, for account-style deployments, Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts with kind: MongoDB). Terraform (azurerm): azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster (or azurerm_cosmosdb_account with the MongoDB API).
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM/Terraform resource type for the managed cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (note spelling 'mongoClusters'). Azure Verified Modules and AzAPI/azurerm examples reference that resource (module names reflect 'mongo-cluster').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters ARM/Bicep docs
Azure Verified Modules: Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) / mongo-cluster module

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used 'mongodbClusters' and conflated older 'databaseAccounts with MongoDB API' patterns; the modern vCore cluster resource is 'mongoClusters'.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM resource name in templates will cause deployment failures.
improvements: Update example IaC snippets in samples and agent skills to the canonical 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' resource name and call out the old 'databaseAccounts' pattern as distinct (for RU-based Cosmos API).

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical connection string (TLS): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<clustername>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<username>@ You can also use mongodb+srv:// when DNS SRV is provided. TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true), and older Cosmos-based endpoints require replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: Authoritative connection-string guidance for Azure DocumentDB clusters uses mongodb+srv:// for SRV-style endpoints and mongodb:// for direct endpoints. Hostnames use '<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com' or '<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com'. TLS (tls=true or ssl=true) must be enabled. Recommended options include authMechanism (SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra), retryWrites=false, and maxIdleTimeMS=120000. Older Cosmos RU-based accounts used '.documents.azure.com' patterns for some older server versions; use the portal-generated connection string for your specific cluster.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB - connection string guidance
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver (node example, mongodb+srv usage)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (documents.azure.com / port 10255) connection-string patterns with current DocumentDB hostnames (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and the SRV usage. The exact form depends on the cluster type and server version; portal-generated strings are authoritative.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos 'documents.azure.com' connection string pattern (for older server versions)

confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding an incorrect connection-string template (wrong host suffix or port) will make the app fail to connect; always use the connection string from the portal or the cluster's provided credentials.
improvements: In the sample README and config template, instruct the developer to copy the exact connection string from the Azure portal or the documentdb MCP 'list-connection-strings' output and avoid hardcoding a pattern.
Document the difference between SRV (mongodb+srv) and standard (mongodb://host:port) connection strings for the cluster on a Learn page or agent-skill snippet the kit uses.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Provisioning is billed by compute tier (vCore-style instance sizes; e.g. M-series tiers like M30) and storage. This service uses provisioned compute (vCores/instance sizes) rather than RU/s for the MongoDB-compatible clusters (serverless options may exist separately).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Azure DocumentDB clusters are billed by compute tier (vCore cluster tiers such as M10, M30, etc.) and provisioned storage. There is not an RU-per-operation billing model for the vCore clusters; compute tier + storage model applies.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute & storage model)

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth: MongoDB-style credentials (SCRAM username/password)... The service also supports X.509 and (in newer builds) AAD/Microsoft Entra authentication where the driver uses an AAD access token (SASL/OAUTHBEARER) obtained from Microsoft Entra and supplied as the authentication mechanism.
confusions.grounded_answer: Authoritative: Azure DocumentDB supports native MongoDB authentication (SCRAM-SHA-256 username/password) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC) authentication. Entra-auth connections use MONGODB-OIDC / authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC in the connection string and may require authMechanismProperties and registered identities; the Learn docs describe using client IDs or managed identities. Public docs show the MONGODB-OIDC pattern and registration flow. X.509 certificate-based authentication is not prominently documented as supported for client data-plane auth in the same way; do not assume X.509 is available for data-plane unless documented for your cluster/tier.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Role-based access control / Entra authentication guidance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer generalized authentication options and mentioned X.509 without a supported Learn page for client certificate-based data-plane auth; the primary documented methods are native SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC).
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to implement X.509 client auth without confirming service support will waste time; choose SCRAM or MONGODB-OIDC per documented guidance.
improvements: Add a short 'Authentication for clients' section in the main DocumentDB Quickstart that lists SCRAM-SHA-256 and MONGODB-OIDC (Entra) with example connection strings and how to register a managed identity.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for synchronous Python; motor for async Python). For ODM in Python use Beanie (which uses Motor). There is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK for application access — use the MongoDB-compatible drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use standard MongoDB drivers. For async Python + ODM, the sample's choice (Beanie backed by Motor) is appropriate. There is no separate 'Azure DocumentDB' app SDK for data-plane operations; use MongoDB drivers and ODMs.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported vector index methods include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Example index creation (MongoDB 7.0-style vector index) with db.products.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { vector: { dimensions: 1536, similarity: "cosine", method: "hnsw", methodOptions: { m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } })
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports IVF, HNSW and DiskANN vector indexes. Index creation on DocumentDB uses a createIndexes runCommand payload with 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' or 'kind' = 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and parameters such as dimensions, similarity metric (COS/L2/IP), and algorithm-specific options (m, efConstruction for HNSW; numLists for IVF; lBuild/lSearch, maxDegree for DiskANN). The service's index creation syntax differs from the plain MongoDB 7 createIndex shape; use the DocumentDB 'createIndexes' command template shown in the vector-search docs.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search guide)
Vector search - diskann / ivf / hnsw examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used MongoDB 7.0-style createIndex vector syntax; DocumentDB exposes vector index creation via a runCommand/createIndexes JSON that uses provider-specific keys (cosmosSearchOptions/kind) and parameter names.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart vector-search examples (DocumentDB) that show 'kind' and cosmosSearchOptions

confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues a MongoDB 7-style createIndex the DocumentDB engine may not accept it; use the documented createIndexes payload to create a working vector index.
improvements: Add an example 'createIndexes' JSON snippet to the DocumentDB agent-skill and the sample README showing the 'kind' parameter and dimensions, and provide a small helper script that creates a vector index with sensible defaults for the sample.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Basic full-text search: use MongoDB text indexes and $text queries. For hybrid (vector + text) search you combine a vector nearest-neighbour stage with text filtering/re-ranking — either via a combined search aggregation stage ($search / knnBeta or a vector-search stage if supported) or by running a vector KNN to get candidates and then applying text filtering or BM25 re-ranking.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides an integrated $search aggregation stage with the 'cosmosSearch' operator that supports vector (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) search and can be combined with filters and text queries (BM25-like behavior) in the same aggregation pipeline. The recommended approach for hybrid search in DocumentDB is to use the built-in cosmosSearch operator in $search for combined vector + lexical filters rather than ad-hoc client-side re-ranking.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store and hybrid search guidance (use cosmosSearch in $search)
Hybrid and filtered vector search examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described community MongoDB text index + client-side re-ranking workflows which are valid generally, but DocumentDB exposes integrated hybrid search primitives (cosmosSearch) that are preferred and more efficient.
confusions.build_risk: Implementing hybrid search with a naive client-side re-rank instead of using cosmosSearch will be slower and miss infrastructure-provided optimizations.
improvements: Add a 'hybrid search' quick example on the vector-search Learn page showing a combined cosmosSearch query with both vector and BM25-like lexical filtering and returning searchScore via $meta.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: The service advertises MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Commonly-missing features in managed MongoDB-compatible offerings include a few admin-level commands, some server parameters, and sometimes features such as server-side file storage (GridFS peculiarities)...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0 and documents that it implements ~99% of user-facing MongoDB operators; some admin and low-level ops are restricted because the platform manages infrastructure. Check the MQL compatibility docs for exact operator-level differences.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB compatibility and supported wire protocol versions
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer named a single supported version (7.0) while the product supports a range of wire-protocol versions (5.0–8.0).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming only MongoDB 7.0 compatibility could cause unnecessary driver/version constraints; the app should detect/target an appropriate wire protocol or driver versions compatible across the supported range.
improvements: Add a compact compatibility table to the Quickstart pages and agent skills showing supported wire-protocol versions 5–8 and recommended driver versions for Python Motor/pymongo/Beanie.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no exact Microsoft emulator ... For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) listening on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides an official local development Docker image 'ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest' and a local gateway that listens on port 10260 (gateway port). The quickstarts and local-development docs show how to pull/run the DocumentDB local image and connect using tls/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates on port 10260. Using a plain mongo:7.0 image is an alternative for very basic driver-level checks but is not the recommended DocumentDB local experience.

grounding_links.title: Development loop: start DocumentDB in Docker and connection details (port 10260)
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB (local image)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer defaulted to the common practice of running official MongoDB docker for local testing; DocumentDB provides its own local gateway image and documented port (10260), which is the correct dev environment to mirror the service features (vector index, special auth modes).
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain mongo:7.0 image for integration tests may miss DocumentDB-specific features (vector index syntax, auth behaviors) and produce false negatives or false assumptions.
improvements: In the local-dev quickstart and agent skills, emphasize the DocumentDB local image and the gateway port 10260 as the recommended local dev path rather than using upstream mongo images.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams require replica-set behavior; many managed MongoDB-compatible clusters support change streams by default. If supported, no additional per-collection flag is typically required, but the account must be configured as a replica-set-capable cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams. For multishard clusters, there is a preview feature 'Change streams for multishard clusters' that can be enabled in the cluster Features settings in the portal; change streams are resumable and support pre-images and other options. For many single-shard clusters, change streams are available by default; multi-shard support requires enabling the preview feature and respecting prerequisites.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (how to enable for multishard clusters, options, pre-images and resume tokens)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer gave a generic MongoDB statement; DocumentDB specifically documents a feature toggle and preview steps for multishard change streams.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams will behave identically without checking cluster-level features (multishard enablement) could cause run-time failures when building streaming workflows or migrations.
improvements: Add a short checklist in the agent kit: 'If you need multishard change streams, enable the cluster feature and ensure Rebalancer is off; otherwise single-shard streams usually work by default.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the dedicated documentdb MCP server (named 'documentdb' in the environment stated). The general Azure MCP server does not expose service-specific data-plane tooling for DocumentDB clusters; use the documentdb MCP server for collection/index inspection and agent tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The environment has a dedicated 'documentdb' MCP server that provides data-plane tools (list/create indexes, aggregate, explain, find, insert, etc.). The general 'azure' MCP server provides control-plane guidance but not the same collection-level data-plane tools.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server tools (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a service called DocumentDB which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (multi-model). 'Azure DocumentDB' historically referred to the original DocumentDB service that became Cosmos DB; the current MongoDB-compatible managed offering is the Cosmos/MongoDB API or a new DocumentDB-branded managed MongoDB. The open-source DocumentDB project is unrelated; the Azure naming overlap is historical.
confusions.grounded_answer: Clarified: The current product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and was renamed; it is distinct from the older 'Azure DocumentDB' (2014–2017) that became Cosmos DB. The current offering is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and the older Cosmos RU-based Mongo API. The naming is historically confusing; Learn docs explicitly clarify these relationships.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? - naming & history clarified
FAQ: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Naming history is complex and the same words ('DocumentDB') were used for multiple, different Microsoft products over time; older blog posts and legacy pages increase the confusion.

confusion_sources.title: Older blog posts and historical docs that conflate 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos DB'

confusions.build_risk: Confusing the services can cause the developer to use the wrong SDK, CLI, or doc set (e.g., using RU-based Cosmos DB APIs vs vCore cluster APIs).
improvements: Add a one-line 'naming map' to the top of the DocumentDB Learn pages and the agent kit explaining: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore; current) = previously Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore). Not the old 2014 DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB; not Amazon DocumentDB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is an Azure-managed, MongoDB-compatible server (an implementation that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol). From application code you should use standard MongoDB drivers and expect small interoperability differences (admin commands, some server parameters or ops-level commands).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project). It speaks the MongoDB wire protocol and is compatible with MongoDB drivers; application code uses standard MongoDB drivers/ODMs but should account for documented platform-level differences (some administrative commands gated or different).

grounding_links.title: What is DocumentDB (in Azure) - engine & implementations
Compare Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB Atlas / engine notes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was roughly correct about driver compatibility but didn't highlight that the engine is DocumentDB (open-source) rather than a vanilla MongoDB server; some admin behaviors are platform-managed.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the engine is 'plain MongoDB' could lead to using admin commands or server features that are blocked or implemented differently on DocumentDB.
improvements: Add a clear 'engine & compatibility' sentence to quickstarts: 'DocumentDB engine (open-source) implements the MongoDB wire protocol; use MongoDB drivers, but check the compatibility matrix for admin operations.'

confusions.question: Which database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_retail_03 for all sample-created collections and data.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment and prompt metadata require the sample to use the database named 'sample_retail_03' for all sample-created collections and data.

confusions.question: Where should the Azure DocumentDB connection string be read from for the sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string at runtime from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and fall back to a config file; do not write the actual secret into files. If missing or invalid, show a clear error and exit.
confusions.grounded_answer: Follow the run-environment guidance: read the connection string from environment (DOCUMENTDB_URI). For developer convenience provide a .env.example (placeholder) and a config/settings module that reads DOCUMENTDB_URI (and returns a clear error if missing). Never write the real secret into repository files.
confusions.build_risk: Storing secrets in repo files would be a security/privacy breach; failing to error when missing would confuse users.
improvements: In the sample README make the environment variable name explicit and include a .env.example with placeholders and a snippet showing how the app reports a missing/invalid connection string.

confusions.question: What vector index definition does this sample need for product embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field. Example (MongoDB 7.0-style) with dimensions 1536, similarity cosine, method hnsw, methodOptions { m:16, efConstruction:200 }.
confusions.grounded_answer: You must create a DocumentDB vector index on the 'embedding' field using the DocumentDB createIndexes runCommand template. Choose the index kind appropriate to the cluster and data size (HNSW or DiskANN are recommended for M30+; IVF may be fine for small demos). Pick dimensions to match the chosen embedding model (the sample must choose and use consistent dims). Example DocumentDB JSON uses 'kind' = 'vector-hnsw' or 'vector-diskann' with parameters (dimensions, similarity: 'COS'/'L2'/'IP', and algorithm-specific options).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index kinds and examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer used MongoDB 7-style createIndex snippet and a guessed dimensions value (1536) without a committed embedding model; DocumentDB requires a specific createIndexes structure and exact dimensions that must match your embedding model.
confusions.build_risk: Creating an index with wrong JSON shape or wrong dimensions will cause indexing errors or invalid vector search results.
improvements: Provide a small helper script in the sample that reads the embedding dimension from a config constant and issues the DocumentDB createIndexes runCommand with correct 'kind' and options, with safe defaults for demo (e.g., HNSW with moderate m/ef).

confusions.question: Which Python client libraries will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Beanie ODM (async) backed by Motor (async pymongo). Use pymongo (or python's motor) for administrative tasks such as index creation if needed. Add packages: beanie, motor, pymongo, fastapi, uvicorn, python-dotenv (or pydantic settings).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use Beanie (ODM) on top of Motor for async app code; pymongo/motor can be used for admin tasks like issuing a createIndexes runCommand if Beanie doesn't expose it conveniently. Include fastapi, uvicorn, python-dotenv or pydantic.BaseSettings for config.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with Python (driver)

confusions.question: What query/aggregation does the sample use to find the 5 nearest alternatives by cosine similarity?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a vector KNN aggregation stage (if supported) such as knnBeta/$vectorSearch. Example aggregation (conceptual): use $vectorSearch/$cosmosSearch to return results with $meta: 'searchScore'. If $vectorSearch/$knn not available, fall back to client-side cosine calculation.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB $search aggregation stage with the cosmosSearch operator and specify the 'vector' argument, the 'path' to the embedding field, 'k':5 and similarity type. Project the 'searchScore' (via $meta: 'searchScore') into results. If the cluster lacks vector-search features (rare on M30+), fallback strategies exist, but the documented approach is the $search/cosmosSearch pattern.

grounding_links.title: Perform a vector similarity search with cosmosSearch in $search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer used generic 'knnBeta' wording from other products; DocumentDB uses cosmosSearch/$search and provider-specific parameters.
confusions.build_risk: Using syntax from another vector DB or Atlas will fail; use the documented cosmosSearch payload.
improvements: Include a concrete $search/cosmosSearch aggregation example in the sample repository and the agent skill so builders copy a working query.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & dimension
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt doesn't fix which embedding model to use (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI or other) and thus the embedding dimensionality. No installed skill provided a default for this sample. The builder must pick a specific model (and match the vector index 'dimensions' to it). Looked in installed skills and Microsoft Learn vector-search docs — they describe index limits and parameter shapes but do not mandate a default model and dims.

information_gaps.title: Index parameter tuning for 10k vectors
information_gaps.description: Optimal index parameters (HNSW m/efConstruction, IVF numLists, DiskANN lBuild/lSearch) for a 10k-vector product dataset are not prescribed by any skill or doc as an explicit recommended default for this exact scale. The vector-search docs describe tuning rules and heuristics, but the builder must choose values (e.g., HNSW m=16/efConstruction=200 is reasonable) and validate with the documentdb MCP explain/statistics tools.

information_gaps.title: Python runtime & dependency pinning
information_gaps.description: Prompt review assumed Python 3.11; the machine has Python 3.13. The sample doesn't specify exact package versions for Beanie/Motor/pymongo compatible with the cluster's wire-protocol versions. No installed skill gave a single pinned requirements.txt for this sample; the builder should choose and test driver versions.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the production cluster's connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (environment); include a .env.example with placeholder, and have the app show a clear error and exit if the env var is missing or if the connection attempt fails.

For local development and integration tests, if you want a local dev gateway that mirrors the service, use the DocumentDB local Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and connect to port 10260 rather than a generic mongo:7 image.
